title: Upper Rio Grande Streamflow, Climate, and Recent Increases in Runoff Efficiency
content:
Abstract

The Rio Grande is the main source of surface water supply for south-central Colorado and much of New Mexico, with obligations via interstate and international treaties to Texas and Mexico. Recent drought conditions exacerbated by a warming climate have increased demand for this limited water supply. Like other snowmelt-dominated watersheds in the western US, this water resource is vulnerable to declining snowpack and earlier melt-off, and the drought conditions over the past two decades have challenged the management of this river system. An examination of key hydroclimatic variables shows that in spite of warm, dry conditions and decreasing snowpack, the Rio Grande headwaters show no significant trend in annual flow, and runoff efficiency shows a positive trend over recent decades. Given this unexpected result, it is important to understand underlying causes of the apparent increase in runoff efficiency to anticipate changes in Rio Grande water supply in the future. Two possible factors are hypothesized: the shift in timing of runoff and the impacts of widespread high-elevation tree mortality due to a spruce beetle epidemic, and both may be playing a role. The increase in runoff efficiency may be short-lived, however, and could already be declining. The Rio Grande headwaters exemplifies the convergence of conditions –including natural climate variability, forest disturbance, and anthropogenic climate change– which may be affecting runoff efficiency in other critical headwaters.
